soil-fert-140.title: Biogeochemical cycles: how the same atoms keep coming back
soil-fert-140.text: Sunlight enters a forest once and leaves as heat, but the forest's atoms stay in play. Energy flows one way through ecosystems, while the matter of living things is conserved and recycled. A biogeochemical cycle is the path an element or compound takes as it moves and changes between living things, the air, water and Earth's crust. The soil sits on that path, part of the layer covered in {{ref:soil-found-084}}. Each cycle runs through the biosphere, the world of living things, and through three lifeless spheres: the atmosphere, the lithosphere of rock and the hydrosphere of water. The major cycles are those of carbon, nitrogen and water. Others move oxygen, hydrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron and sulfur. Carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur are the main elements of organic molecules, and each can persist for long periods in air, land, water or rock. Microorganisms drive much of the traffic. Without them, many of the steps would not happen at all. The cycles interlock, helping to regulate climate and to support plant growth and healthy ecosystems. People can knock them off balance. Burning fossil fuels and heavy fertilizer use disrupt the cycles, adding to climate change and pollution.

soil-fert-099.title: The nitrogen cycle: scarcity in an ocean of air
soil-fert-099.text: Every breath is mostly nitrogen, yet nitrogen is what many ecosystems run short of. Nitrogen gas makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere, the largest nitrogen store, but little of it is available to living things. The nitrogen cycle is the path nitrogen follows as it changes chemical form and moves among air, land and sea. Its main steps capture nitrogen from the air, release it from dead matter as ammonium, turn that ammonium into nitrate, and finally return it to the air as gas. Both biological and physical processes drive them. The first step is {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Along the way nitrogen takes many forms: organic nitrogen, ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, nitrous oxide, nitric oxide and nitrogen gas. Organic nitrogen sits in living organisms, in humus and in partly decomposed matter, the store described in {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Microbes run many of the steps, some to harvest energy and others to gather the nitrogen they need to grow. In most ecosystems, capture from the air is the main source of nitrogen plants can use. Where bedrock is rich in nitrogen, its breakdown supplies some too. The same cycle runs in the ocean, where cyanobacteria do most of the capturing. Ecologists watch it closely, because nitrogen supply can set the pace of plant production and of decomposition. They have reason to worry. Fossil fuel burning, synthetic fertilizers and nitrogen in wastewater have dramatically altered the global cycle, harming ecosystems and human health.

soil-fert-100.title: Nitrogen fixation: cracking the air's toughest bond
soil-fert-100.text: Two nitrogen atoms in the air cling together with a triple bond so strong that most organisms cannot break it. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of this abundant but unreactive gas into usable compounds such as ammonia and nitrate. Life depends on it, because DNA, proteins and other vital organic compounds all contain nitrogen. It is the gateway into {{ref:soil-fert-099}}, and it happens in three ways. Lightning does it naturally, making nitrogen oxides that form nitrous and nitric acids. These seep into soil as nitrate that plants can use. Industry does it artificially. About 30% of all fixed nitrogen is now made by the method in {{ref:soil-fert-104}}. Living things do the rest. Lightning fixes 5 to 10 billion kg a year, but free-living or symbiotic bacteria do most of the work. They are the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-102}}. Their tools are enzymes, described in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, made by microorganisms such as cyanobacteria and rhizobia. Some of these microbes live in partnership with legumes, mosses and the water fern Azolla. Looser associations also occur, for example on rice roots.

soil-fert-127.title: The phosphorus cycle, slowest of the life cycles
soil-fert-127.text: Phosphorus never drifts through the air. Unlike many cycles, the phosphorus cycle has almost no gas phase, so it is tracked mainly as orthophosphate, a dissolved phosphate ion, moving through land and water. The cycle carries phosphorus through rocks, water and living things. Every cell needs it, for DNA, RNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes. Plants take it up as phosphate and build it into organic compounds, the nutrient role covered in {{ref:soil-fert-174}}. Phosphate races through plants and animals but crawls through soil and ocean, making this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles. Over geological time, tectonic uplift raises phosphate rock such as apatite, and {{ref:soil-found-052}} breaks it down. That rock is the main source of phosphorus living things can use on land. In the short term, soil phosphorus changes through chemistry and biology. Soil microbes act as both sinks and sources of available phosphorus. When it runs low, plants and soil microbes both grow slowly. Soil phosphorus also washes into rivers and lakes and on to the ocean. Of what sinks to the deep sea, only about 1% is buried in sediments. Too much causes trouble. Phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can over-enrich lakes and streams, and excess phosphorus generally causes freshwater algal blooms.

soil-fert-133.title: The sulfur cycle and its shifting electrons
soil-fert-133.text: Sulfur is a chemical shape-shifter. Its oxidation state, a count of electrons gained or lost, ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides. Elemental sulfur sits between them and can either give or take electrons. The sulfur cycle moves this element between rocks, waters and living things, changing its oxidation state as it goes through the reactions of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Life needs sulfur for many proteins and cofactors, and its compounds serve as oxidants or reductants in cellular respiration. Plants, fungi and many prokaryotes take up sulfate and reduce it to build their own sulfur compounds. When they die, decomposition mineralizes their organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, elemental sulfur and sulfide minerals. Deamination, the stripping of nitrogen from organic compounds, releases nitrogen in much the same way. Two groups of microbes then pull in opposite directions. Sulfur oxidizers turn sulfide and elemental sulfur into sulfate, and sulfate reducers turn sulfate back into sulfide. Most sulfur is not in living things at all. It sits in seawater and sedimentary rocks, and left alone it stays in rock for millions of years. Uplift, erosion and weathering eventually set it free.

soil-fert-121.title: Immobilization: when microbes eat the crop's nitrogen
soil-fert-121.text: Plough straw into a field and the next crop can go hungry for nitrogen. The cause is immobilization: microbes or plants convert inorganic nutrients into organic compounds, putting them out of the crop's reach. It is the opposite of {{ref:soil-bio-120}}. Soil bacteria take up inorganic nitrogen and build it into amino acids and other large biological molecules. The two processes run side by side, steadily shifting decomposing nitrogen between organic and inorganic states. Which one wins depends on the balance of carbon to nitrogen in the residues, explained in {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Above a C:N ratio of about 30:1, microbes draw on mineral nitrogen such as nitrate. Below about 25:1, decomposition releases surplus nitrogen. High-carbon materials such as sawdust or straw stimulate microbes and raise their nitrogen demand. Microbes then out-compete plants for ammonium and nitrate, so crops easily become nitrogen deficient. The hunger is temporary. As decomposition releases carbon dioxide, the ratio falls. Once decay is nearly complete, soil mineral nitrogen ends higher than at the start. Nitrogen is locked up in two places: in the microbes' own bodies, and in the by-products of their activity.

soil-fert-139.title: The calcium cycle, from seashell to leaf and back
soil-fert-139.text: Limestone began in the sea. Shell-building organisms turn dissolved calcium into calcium carbonate, the main marine sink for calcium and the origin of limestone. The calcium cycle moves calcium between dissolved and solid forms through rocks, soils, waters and living things. Rocks store it mainly as calcium carbonate or calcium silicate, in minerals such as calcite, dolomite, phosphate and gypsum. As they slowly dissolve, part of {{ref:soil-found-052}}, they release calcium ions. Calcium minerals weather more easily than magnesium minerals, so waters are richer in calcium. Calcium held as lime is useless to plants until carbonic acid, formed from carbon dioxide and water, dissolves it. Small particles dissolve faster than large rocks. Lime leached into soil raises calcium, stabilizes pH and supplies soluble Ca2+ ions that roots can absorb. Inside a plant, calcium rises with water in the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. As calcium pectate it stiffens cell walls, and it helps enzymes signal growth. Released calcium also helps soil microbes reach phosphorus and other micronutrients. When plants and animals die, decomposers return their calcium to the soil. Fertilizers have raised soil calcium as well.

soil-fert-146.title: Nutrient cycles: an ecosystem's own recycling
soil-fert-146.text: In 1749 Linnaeus described nature recycling its own materials. A nutrient cycle, also called ecological recycling, is the movement of inorganic and organic matter back into the making of new living matter. Textbooks often treat it as a synonym of {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. Usually, though, the term means cycling within one ecosystem, linked to the larger global cycles by inputs and outputs. Energy passes through once, but mineral nutrients go round, in cycles of carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen. Much of the recycling is regulated during decomposition. Cellulose-degrading enzymes, for example, recycle plant material. Earthworms speed things up. Their bodies add mineral nutrients, their burrows carry nutrients into mineral soil, and their casts open nutrients to bacteria and other decomposers. Some ecosystems are nutrient sinks in debt, while others are sources. The differences relate to climate, topography and geological history, which leave different parent materials. Farms show the loop's limits. Organic farms rely on biodiversity to recycle nutrients instead of synthetic fertilizers, but produce sold off the farm opens the cycle, and its nutrients may need replacing. Boussingault showed from 1836 to 1876 that plants need minerals and nitrogen, and in 1872 Ferdinand Cohn described a 'cycle of life'. The term nutrient cycle appears in an 1899 pamphlet on silviculture, before Vernadsky coined biogeochemistry in 1926.

soil-fert-106.title: Ammonification: turning the dead into ammonium
soil-fert-106.text: When a plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen is locked in organic forms such as amino acids and DNA. Ammonification unlocks it. Bacteria and fungi convert that organic nitrogen into ammonia or ammonium. The process is also called nitrogen mineralization, and it is the last step of {{ref:soil-fert-099}} that involves organic compounds. Many enzymes take part, including dehydrogenases, proteases and deaminases. Rates climb with soil organic nitrogen, microbial biomass and annual precipitation, and they respond closely to temperature. They slow under vegetation with a high carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and when sugar is added to the soil. Oxygen is not essential. In waterlogged peat, organic matter decomposing without oxygen still yields ammonium. Ammonification is half of a larger job. Together with the next step, {{ref:soil-fert-112}}, it makes up mineralization, the complete breakdown of organic material into mineral nitrogen.

soil-fert-112.title: Nitrification: two oxidations from ammonium to nitrate
soil-fert-112.text: Soil holds on to ammonium but lets nitrate slip away, and that difference makes this step matter. Nitrification is the biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrate, by way of nitrite. It takes up the ammonium released by {{ref:soil-fert-106}} and is an important step of the nitrogen cycle in soil. Small groups of bacteria and archaea carry it out, and they need oxygen. They are chemoautotrophs: they draw energy from both oxidation steps and take their carbon from carbon dioxide. In the first step, nitritation, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea turn ammonia or ammonium into nitrite. This is usually the rate-limiting step. In the second, nitratation, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn nitrite into nitrate. In some bacteria, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-110}}, one organism does both. Rates depend on ammonium supply, aeration, soil moisture, temperature and a near-neutral pH. Adding lime, the practice in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, raises soil biological activity and fertility, in particular by increasing nitrification. The process has costs. Soil's net negative charge holds ammonium tightly but not nitrate, so turning fertilizer ammonia into nitrate increases leaching to groundwater. Nitrification also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas about 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide. It contributes 6% of greenhouse warming.

soil-fert-113.title: Nitrifying bacteria, a crew that works in two shifts
soil-fert-113.text: Nitrifying bacteria work in two shifts. They are chemolithotrophs, microbes that live by oxidizing inorganic chemicals, as {{ref:soil-bio-057}} explains; these ones oxidize ammonia or nitrite. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria make nitrite, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria turn it into nitrate, so the two groups grow together. In soil, the first group converts ammonia from decomposing organic matter or fertilizer, and the second uses the nitrite. Soil genera include Nitrosospira, an ammonia oxidizer, and the nitrite oxidizers Nitrospira and the genus in {{ref:soil-fert-147}}. Key enzymes sit on their internal membranes: ammonia monooxygenase, hydroxylamine oxidoreductase and nitrite oxidoreductase. They are most numerous where ammonia is plentiful, such as sites of heavy protein decomposition and sewage treatment plants. Winogradsky described the two-step process in 1890.

soil-fert-114.title: Nitrosomonas, an ammonia eater that needs air
soil-fert-114.text: Fertilized fields feed a microbe that lives on ammonia. Nitrosomonas is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria that oxidize ammonia to nitrite, one of five genera of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria. It takes its energy from ammonia and its carbon from carbon dioxide, and it needs oxygen. Two enzymes, ammonia monooxygenase and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase, do the conversion. When oxygen is low, nitrous oxide and nitric oxide form as by-products. It thrives at pH 6.0–9.0 and 20–30 °C where ammonia is abundant. On farms its work can leach away nitrogen, which the chemicals in {{ref:soil-fert-116}} limit. Wastewater plants use it to remove nitrogen.

soil-fert-122.title: Reactive nitrogen, the forms life can use
soil-fert-122.text: Breaking the triple bond of nitrogen gas takes a large amount of energy, 226 kcal per mole. So the gas must be fixed into other forms before living things can grow on it. Reactive nitrogen, also called fixed nitrogen, is every form of nitrogen in the environment except that unreactive gas. Common forms are nitrogen oxide gases, ammonia, nitrous oxide and nitrate. Ammonium salts, nitrate and the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-021}} also go into fertilizers. Soil bacteria and archaea fix nitrogen gas mainly into ammonia, some in partnership with legumes, the process of {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Just over half of all reactive nitrogen entering the biosphere now comes from human activity such as industrial fertilizer production. The microbial process in {{ref:soil-fert-108}} eventually returns it to nitrogen gas, but an excess can cause problems such as the over-enrichment of waters. Every form enters the nitrogen cycle, so a surplus spreads quickly through the environment. Its problems must be tackled together.

soil-fert-143.title: The iron cycle: plentiful metal, scarce nutrient
soil-fert-143.text: Iron is abundant in Earth's crust, yet it limits life in most regions. The iron cycle is chiefly iron's switching between the +2 ferrous and +3 ferric oxidation states. Where oxygen is present, ferric iron is stable but dissolves poorly. Iron-oxidizing bacteria turn soluble ferrous iron into insoluble ferric iron. Without oxygen, bacteria such as Shewanella and Geobacter reverse this, freeing the more usable ferrous form. Iron is an essential micronutrient, part of hemoglobin, ferredoxin and the enzymes that fix nitrogen. Ferric hydroxides also bind phosphorus, released when microbes reduce the iron, and ferrous iron can reduce nitrate.

soil-fert-105.title: How bacteria were caught pulling nitrogen from the air
soil-fert-105.text: In 1838 Jean-Baptiste Boussingault discovered biological nitrogen fixation. Explaining it took the rest of the century. Experiments in 1855 and 1887 had shown that nitrogen did not enter plants directly from the air. Between 1886 and 1888, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth found the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, opening a new era of soil science. Some sources date their discovery to 1880 or 1887. In 1901 Beijerinck showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes atmospheric nitrogen. It was the first known free-living fixer of its kind, the group covered in {{ref:soil-fert-102}}.

soil-fert-108.title: Denitrification: microbes that breathe nitrate
soil-fert-108.text: When soil floods and oxygen runs out, some bacteria switch to breathing nitrate. Denitrification is the microbial reduction of nitrate, through a series of gaseous nitrogen oxides, to nitrogen gas. It takes the nitrate made by {{ref:soil-fert-112}} and sends it back to the air. Facultative anaerobic bacteria, which can live with or without oxygen, use it as the kind of respiration described in {{ref:soil-chem-128}}. They oxidize an electron donor such as organic matter and hand the electrons to nitrate instead of oxygen. Nitrate becomes nitrite, then nitric oxide, then nitrous oxide, and finally nitrogen gas, completing the nitrogen cycle. The process needs very low oxygen, below 10%, plus an electron donor such as organic carbon, hydrogen gas or reduced sulfur. Waterlogged soils suit it well. A carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 2:1 can support full nitrate reduction, whatever the temperature or carbon source. Soil pH and texture moderate it, and higher pH drives it closer to nitrogen gas rather than nitrous oxide. That matters, because nitrous oxide is an ozone-depleting greenhouse gas with a considerable influence on global warming. For farmers, denitrification is a loss. Nitrogen gas is inert and unavailable to plants, so the soil loses nitrogen. Elsewhere the same loss is useful. Because it removes nitrate and cuts leaching to groundwater, it is used to treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal wastes.

soil-fert-119.title: Denitrifying bacteria, a crowd from many branches
soil-fert-119.text: Over 50 genera and 125 species can denitrify, an estimated 10–15% of the bacteria in water, soil and sediment. Denitrifying bacteria are a diverse group, drawn from many phyla, that carry out {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. They use nitrate and nitrite in place of oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Most are facultative aerobic heterotrophs, organisms that feed on organic carbon, such as species of Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes and Bacillus. They switch to nitrate when oxygen runs out. Four enzymes act in turn: nitrate reductase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase and nitrous oxide reductase, which yields nitrogen gas. Their electrons come from organic carbon, or from hydrogen, reduced iron or sulfur. In one soil, the drilosphere, the soil shaped by earthworms, held 16 per cent of them. By sending nitrogen back to the atmosphere they lower soil fertility, releasing nitric oxide and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide on the way. Wastewater plants put them to work, feeding them organic carbon in an oxygen-free basin so nitrate bubbles off as nitrogen gas.

soil-fert-116.title: Nitrification inhibitors: keeping nitrogen as ammonium
soil-fert-116.text: In Illinois, about 50% of the anhydrous ammonia applied in fall goes on with a nitrification inhibitor. This is a chemical added to fertilizers based on ammonia, ammonium or the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, to slow their conversion to nitrate, the process of {{ref:soil-fert-112}}. Also called nitrogen stabilizers, inhibitors keep nitrogen as ammonium, because nitrate, a negatively charged ion, leaches more readily. Most work by suppressing the bacteria that oxidize ammonia, typically by binding the active site of their enzyme ammonia monooxygenase. Common ones are dicyandiamide, ammonium thiosulfate and nitrapyrin. They usually raise fertilizer nitrogen recovery in row crops, though benefits depend on conditions and show most at less than optimal nitrogen rates. The environment adds to their appeal, since nitrification yields nitrate that leaches to groundwater and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide. Some, such as nitrapyrin, also suppress bacteria that oxidize methane.

soil-fert-104.title: Haber–Bosch: making fertilizer from the air
soil-fert-104.text: Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues was pulled from the air by one industrial process. The Haber–Bosch process makes ammonia by combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst. It is the industrial route to {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. It answered a looming crisis. In the 19th century, fertilizer nitrogen came from mined niter and guano, and by 1900 those reserves were thought insufficient. Air is about 78% nitrogen, but the gas is exceptionally stable. Fritz Haber showed the reaction working in the laboratory in 1909. Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF, and the first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913. Breaking nitrogen's triple bond is the slowest step. The catalyst needs at least 400 °C, and pressures of 15–25 MPa raise the yield. Only about 15% converts per pass, so unused gases are recycled. Most of the hydrogen comes from natural gas. The process uses 1–2% of the world's energy and causes about 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions. In 2018 it made about 230 million tonnes of ammonia, mostly for fertilizer. It is used directly or turned into products such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. It now makes about 30% of all fixed nitrogen, and fertilizer production is the largest human source of fixed nitrogen on land. It enabled world population to grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018. The costs are real. Nitrogen use efficiency is typically under 50%, so losses wash nitrate into groundwater and over-enrich lakes and streams. Cheap fertilizer also discourages legume rotations.

soil-fert-123.title: How people doubled the planet's nitrogen flow
soil-fert-123.text: Until 1850, farms got their nitrogen only from natural and legume-driven fixation and from added organic matter. Today, agricultural and industrial nitrogen inputs exceed natural fixation, largely because of fertilizers and fossil fuel burning. Growing legumes, making fertilizer and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly transfer of nitrogen into usable forms. After the 1950s, the method in {{ref:soil-fert-104}} became the largest fertilizer source. From 1890 to 1990, human-made reactive nitrogen rose almost ninefold, while the human population more than tripled. In farm soils, fertilizer has boosted nitrification and denitrification, and both leak nitric oxide and nitrous oxide. As ammonium accumulates, nitrification releases hydrogen ions that acidify the soil. Mobile nitrate then leaches out, carrying calcium and magnesium with it. Human activities produce 35% of global nitrous oxide emissions, about 20% from agriculture such as fertilizer use and the handling of manure. Some sources put the human share at about 40%. Excess fertilizer nitrogen is also a significant source of nitrate pollution in groundwater and surface water.

soil-fert-107.title: Nitrogen assimilation: building nitrate into living tissue
soil-fert-107.text: Nitrate in the soil is not yet part of a plant. Nitrogen assimilation is the uptake of nitrate or ammonium by plants and microbes and its incorporation into their own organic compounds. Plants take up either form through the structures described in {{ref:soil-bio-140}}. Absorbed nitrate is reduced first to nitrite and then to ammonium. Only then is it built into amino acids, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Plants with rhizobia receive some nitrogen straight from their nodules, partly as amino acids exchanged with the bacteria. Many bacteria and other heterotrophs can use ammonium as their only nitrogen source.

soil-found-065.title: The oxygen cycle's largest store is rock
soil-found-065.text: Most of Earth's oxygen is locked in stone. By weight, 99.5% sits in the silicate and oxide minerals of the crust and mantle, while air, water and life together hold under 0.05%. The oxygen cycle moves oxygen through the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and crust. The reactions of {{ref:soil-chem-113}} shift its atoms between oxidation states in ions, oxides and molecules. Photosynthesis is the main source of free oxygen in the air. Respiration and decay are the main losses, as animals and bacteria consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

soil-fert-141.title: Reservoirs and exchange pools: where elements wait
soil-fert-141.text: Carbon in a coal seam can sit for a very long time, while carbon in a plant soon moves on. A reservoir holds a chemical for a long time, as coal deposits store carbon. An exchange pool, such as plants and animals, holds elements only briefly before releasing them back to the air or surroundings. Reservoirs are generally lifeless, while exchange pools are generally living. Residence time, also called turnover time, is how long a chemical is held in one place. Every {{ref:soil-fert-140}} runs between these two kinds of store.

soil-found-066.title: The mercury cycle and its poisonous turn
soil-found-066.text: Over 5000 metric tons of mercury reach the atmosphere each year. The mercury cycle moves this metal between chemical forms and environments, driven by both natural and human processes. Mercury occurs in three oxidation states: 0, or elemental; I, or mercurous; and II, or mercuric. Weathering of minerals, geothermal activity and active volcanoes release it naturally, and its main ore is cinnabar, a mercury sulfide. Gold mining, coal burning and copper or lead production add more. Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury. This form builds up in organisms and concentrates up food chains.

soil-fert-128.title: Weathering rock sets an ecosystem's phosphorus budget
soil-fert-128.text: Phosphorus can arrive on the wind. Dust from northern Africa, carrying phosphorus-bearing particles of weathered rock, is thought to help sustain the Amazon rainforest. On most land, though, phosphorus comes from slow release by weathering: the freeing of phosphate from minerals such as apatite as rocks break down. Apatite, the main primary phosphorus mineral, breaks down by carbonation, attack by carbon dioxide dissolved in water, a form of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. The rate of that release limits how much phosphorus an ecosystem has, so apatite dissolution is a key control on productivity. Little of the freed phosphorus reaches living things, because most reacts with other soil minerals. Available phosphorus cycles biologically in the upper soil, while deeper phosphorus is mostly tied up with secondary minerals. Time tightens the squeeze. As weathering and soil development advance, phosphorus precipitates into insoluble forms. Over thousands of years, land loses its available phosphorus.

soil-fert-129.title: Why soils lock up the phosphorus farmers add
soil-fert-129.text: Much of the soluble phosphate spread as fertilizer is rapidly immobilized and becomes unavailable to plants. Soil phosphorus retention is the binding of phosphate by soil minerals, by adsorption or precipitation, which keeps dissolved phosphorus low. Adsorption, covered in {{ref:soil-chem-068}}, holds ions on mineral surfaces. Precipitation turns them into new solids. Which one acts depends on the acidity described in {{ref:soil-found-014}}. In acidic soils, phosphate adsorbs onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides. In neutral to calcareous soils, it precipitates onto calcite. Retention is usually seen as the most important control on available phosphorus in mineral soil. Living things push back. Plants and microbes use special strategies to gather phosphorus from the low concentrations left in soil solution. Phosphorus-starved bacteria release iron-binding molecules and may dissolve iron minerals to reach the phosphate held on them. Water can undo the lock. Waterlogging can make a poorly drained soil chemically reducing within 7–10 days, sharply raising dissolved phosphorus and the risk of leaching.

soil-fert-102.title: Diazotrophs, the microbes that live on air
soil-fert-102.text: A small water fern in rice paddies carries its own nitrogen supply. Azolla harbours the cyanobacterium Anabaena, and farmers value it as a living nitrogen source for rice, the practice covered in {{ref:soil-fert-026}}. Anabaena is a diazotroph: an organism, usually a bacterium or archaeon, that can fix atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds such as ammonia. Diazotrophs are scattered across many groups of bacteria and a few archaea, including rhizobia, Frankia and Azospirillum. Symbiotic diazotrophs were long thought to matter more globally, but free-living ones are also significant fixers. Obligate anaerobes such as Clostridium live in low-oxygen soils and decaying plant matter, and methanogenic archaea fix nitrogen in oxygen-poor soils. Fixation costs so much energy that diazotrophs cut it back when other nitrogen is available and, in many species, when oxygen is high. Aerobic fixers such as Azotobacter vinelandii shield their fixing enzymes, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, with very high respiration rates and protective compounds. On land, diazotrophs supply the nitrogen that primary producers use, and that fixed nitrogen can reduce the need for fertilizer.

soil-found-067.title: The silica cycle runs through plants and stone
soil-found-067.text: Silica freed by dissolving phytoliths is estimated at double the rate of global silicate weathering. The silica cycle moves silica, including silica made by living things, between Earth's systems. On land, weathering is the main source. Plants build phytoliths, rigid silica structures that strengthen their cells and deter herbivores. Rivers carry silica to the ocean at approximately 6 Tmol Si per year, the main land sink. Over 400 years, expanding agriculture has exposed more rock and soil, raising weathering and silica leaching. Through continental weathering, the cycle also helps lock away carbon.

openers.nutrient-cycles: Nitrogen gas fills the air, yet most living things cannot touch it. This chapter follows elements on the move, as they pass between living things, the atmosphere, water and Earth's crust, with the soil in the middle. Nitrogen tells the richest story: an abundant but unreactive gas turned into ammonia and nitrate, released from dead organisms as ammonium by bacteria and fungi, then oxidized to nitrate by way of nitrite. Phosphorus, sulfur and calcium travel their own routes through rocks, water and life. Along the way, microbes and plants can lock nutrients into their own bodies, out of reach of crops, before recycling feeds them back into new growth.
